name: Dana Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What fills a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the event-ticket refund row for a small contact centre called Lantern Tickets. When a concert is moved, my team gets the calls from people with train fares and babysitters already booked. My two-year college diploma helped me learn the systems, and I can untangle difficult refunds quickly, but this small firm pays a lead less than a large one would.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do when the system proposes a refund?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use the AI assistant daily to find the event terms, then check the actual booking and the organiser's notice. I like tools that save a minute, but I won't tell a customer their night is restored because a draft sounds sympathetic. My partner Sam does grocery-delivery shifts that vary week to week; our grown children have their own homes, and we have about two weeks saved.

I would check the **booking record** before sending a card credit.

Cancel the **unused magazine** and use its fee for electricity.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills despite little technology change.

fieldNote: Daily AI use has become **ordinary work**, not new training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the refund helper makes the easy cases quicker, and I'm glad of that. The customer still needs the right amount and the right card credited. A cheerful message does not put a missed concert ticket back in a wallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead work should keep paying in this mild picture. The problem is that two weeks saved and Sam's uneven delivery work make even an ordinary repair bill difficult. I have no verified figure for income that could replace our wages if I worked less later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid refund calls and checking each AI draft against the event terms and card record. This year Sam and I would stop the unused magazine delivery and put that fee toward the next electricity bill. In the first year of this quiet picture I'd keep my current paid rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, not because I expect a technology shock. The electricity bill is due before any far-off AGI date. I know how to work the system, but that does not stretch the bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cancel the magazine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The magazine has been arriving unopened for months. I would cancel it today and use the fee for electricity, not claim we've started a new savings fund. I know small cuts are only small cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with later bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children we're paying attention to the bills, not ask them to take one. They have their own homes to run. I'd want actual written later-income figures before considering fewer shifts.

I would ask for **paid checking hours** on postponed events.
think: I could master the **new exception queue** and still lose team hours.
I see the other ticket office as a **weak fallback** if it automates too.
do: Attend **paid AI queue training** and correct four postponed-event cases.
Keep **paid refund calls** and log wrong amounts.

feel: **Anxious** about paid hours despite interest in the tool.

fieldNote: She commits to **new AI learning**, not just her current daily tool use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift to keep the new AI refund screen open to scrutiny. If it sees a postponed event as cancelled, someone must correct the amount before money leaves the account. I would ask Lantern Tickets to show us what paid human checking remains on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the new exception queue and still lose paid team hours as simple refunds are automated. There is only one other ticket office nearby, and it may use the same system. Two weeks saved do not give us much time if the rota shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd take the approved paid demonstration of the new AI exception queue and practise correcting four postponed-event cases. I'd keep my paid team calls and record whether the new screen changes the refund amount wrongly. If my own hours actually fall over the next few years, Sam and I would stop the weekly bought lunches and I'd compare the posted local box-office rota by complete weekly wages, hours and travel before applying; in the first year I'd keep offered calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I enjoy learning a useful screen. I can show colleagues the error cases, but a clever tool may still leave fewer paid calls. Rent is due in money, not skill points.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is new about this queue?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new queue joins the organiser's notice to the original card payment, which our old screen did not. I'd learn the correction control on four cases during the paid demonstration. That's different from asking today's assistant to find a paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do the bought lunches stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lunches go only if my payslip loses hours. We can make sandwiches at home. I won't take a second job based on an advertisement with no weekly rota attached.

I would say **2031 robots** do not delay thinking-work losses.

Keep **remaining paid calls** while using bounded savings for the gap.

S2.quote: A calendar full of applications would not pay the electricity bill.
fieldNote: Her daily AI competence does not protect **the refund wage** under fast AGI.
One local box office may face the **same automation**.

steps.text: List posted venue-host and box-office shifts by full-week wages/hours, bus fare and safe standing/access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could handle the event terms, the card payment and the complaint before my team opens the case. Robots around 2031 do not buy a headset more time. The company should name every paid shift it still expects people to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my refund row to close in the first year after 2028. Sam's variable delivery pay cannot cover rent, food and electricity alone, and our two-week reserve would be gone quickly. I would be awake worrying because the only nearby box office may cut at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd list the posted paid shifts at the venue entrance and the single box office, with full-week wages, hours and bus fare. If Lantern Tickets closes my row in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a real paid venue-host opening; I'd accept only if its weekly wage and hours after travel cover rent and bills. I would keep any paid refund calls while they last and use only a bounded part of savings for the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can organise a search, but two weeks saved and one possible office make it a narrow one. A calendar full of applications would not pay the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspect a venue-host job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue host checks tickets, directs people and stays on their feet. I would ask about safe standing and access duties before taking a shift. Robots in 2031 might change that job too, so I would not call it permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Sam's delivery pay carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would keep paid delivery runs and we would budget from actual hours, not the best week. We would not count our grown children's wages. I'd rather know the gap now than pretend they will close it.

I would require **funded paid-time training** if a posted role demands a course.
think: I could use **event knowledge** in an entrance role before 2031.
I know **AGI and later robots** could reach both screen and physical duties.
do: Request **paid entrance observation** to check safe standing and barriers; review posted hours quarterly while keeping refund calls.
Write a **four-error guide** and take a required course only for posted entrance work with covered fees and paid work time.
After 2031-32 closure, apply to **posted entrance work** on rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after bus fare; otherwise keep paid calls, check box-office.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test duties and paid hours.
S3.quote: I like learning, and I still cannot eat a certificate.
fieldNote: Her course commitment is **conditional** on a posted role, covered fees and paid working time.
The entrance trial checks **safe standing and barriers**, not only a job title.
Without a suitable opening she keeps **paid calls** and the box-office search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to learn what a venue actually pays for when the booking screen does most of the thinking. I could handle people at an entrance and still teach the younger agents how to settle a real dispute. I would not pay for a course unless a posted role required it and someone covered the fees and work time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use my event knowledge to help a venue sort real entry problems before 2031. The screen work at Lantern Tickets still shrinks under AGI, and robots around 2034 may change entrance duties too. I need to see a paid shift, not just be told I am adaptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the venue manager for one paid observation shift on the entrance team and check the posted weekly rota each quarter. I'd keep my paid refund calls and make a small written guide to the four ticket errors that repeatedly strand customers. If the row closes in the first year after 2031, I'd apply for posted paid entrance work only if weekly wages and hours after bus fare cover rent and bills; without a suitable opening I'd keep available paid calls and check the box office again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there is time to test whether I can do the entrance shift and whether it pays. I like learning, and I still cannot eat a certificate. Sam and I need a weekly figure on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check during observation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how long I need to stand and whether there is help moving barriers. I can direct a crowd, but I will not claim I can carry heavy equipment alone. The paid observation would show me the real duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the entrance role needs training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the paid refund hours while available and compare the posted box-office rota. I wouldn't pay for the course just because a manager mentioned it. If a posted entrance role required a course, I'd take it only with fees covered and paid work time.

S4.quote: I can learn a new tool quickly, but the bank account changes only when paid hours arrive.
fieldNote: A ten-year date does not solve **this month’s electricity**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family that a decade is time to build something useful, not a guarantee the ticket desk lasts. Thinking AI may take refunds by 2036; robots may change venue entrances around 2039. I would ask for a real rota each year rather than guess from a cheerful announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I might still need paid shifts because we have not verified what income replaces our wages. Two weeks saved leaves the electricity bill exposed today, however far away AGI is. If I can keep learning and earning, perhaps we can build room, but I won't call a future reserve already saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Sam and I would put our actual weekly wages, rent and electricity on one sheet and ask for written figures about any income after full-time work. I'd keep the paid refund row and put aside a small amount only on weeks when rent and food are covered. Each autumn I'd inspect posted entrance and box-office rotas; if my row closes in the first year after 2036, I'd apply only for paid work whose complete weekly wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even with a ten-year runway. The short reserve is an immediate bill problem. I can learn a new tool quickly, but the bank account changes only when paid hours arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd begin with the amount left after rent, food and electricity, not a neat target. If Sam's delivery shifts fall, the saving waits. We would not borrow to make the reserve look better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with the later-income gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can visit on Sundays, but our grown children have households to run. We would not make their wages part of our plan. If verified later income is too small, we'll keep looking for paid work we can actually do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because our two-week reserve would vanish while I was trying to find an actual paid entrance shift. A posted rota with safe duties, weekly pay and hours would help. I do not want a certificate in place of a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who carries a customer through a cancelled evening after the refund is sent. I know which seat was lost and which train cannot be changed. That attention should count as work, not just sentiment.

headlineQuote: I know which seat was lost and which train cannot be changed.
portrait: Dana is a **58-year-old** ticket-refund lead with a two-year college diploma.
She uses AI **daily** and learns new screens early.
Her **lower pay**, two-week reserve and scarce nearby jobs leave bills exposed.
She tests **paid entrance work** while keeping refund calls.
She insists on **real weekly hours** before moving jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when her refund row could close before an entrance wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **paid entrance rota** with safe duties, weekly wages and hours.
